title: Security Analysis of Ekert-type QKD Protocol Coming Under Cloning Attacks
abstract: We analyze the security of an Ekert type bipartite key distribution protocol coming under cloning attacks by an untrusted observer. Precisely, an eavesdropper is assumed to intercept and apply an asymmetric, phase-variant cloner on one or both qubits which are transmitted over public channel from an authenticated source to the trusted parties. We partially characterize two-qubit states from the perspective of designing a QKD protocol that can generate a distillable secret key among the trusted users even under such cloning attacks. We rely upon Devetak Winter framework for computing key rate so as to identify states, which when used in the protocol, secret-key can be distilled. Utility of an entangled state, for designing a successful QKD protocol, changes from single-qubit to double-qubits cloning attacks. Interestingly, we can distinguish some useful families of two-qubit entangled states when only one of the transmitted qubits is cloned by a malicious third party.
summary: This work provides a rigorous security analysis of Ekert-type QKD protocols against cloning attacks by calculating the distillable key rate using the Devetak-Winter framework. It demonstrates that simply passing standard quantum checks is insufficient for security, as the key rate must remain positive even when the eavesdropper performs complex cloning operations on the transmitted qubits.
main_problem: The paper analyzes the security of Ekert-type Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) protocols when subjected to cloning attacks by an untrusted eavesdropper.
main_result: The distillable secret key rate ($r_D$) must be calculated using the Devetak-Winter framework, showing that passing standard checks (like Bell violation) is insufficient for guaranteeing security against cloning.
method: The security is quantified by calculating the Devetak-Winter key rate, $r_D = \sum (I(A:B) - \chi(A:E))$, which must be positive for a secret key to be distilled.
model_or_system: The analysis focuses on bipartite entangled two-qubit states ($ho_{AB}$) shared between two trusted parties (A and B), subjected to asymmetric, phase-variant cloning attacks on one or both qubits.
key_observables: Distillable secret key rate ($r_D$), Mutual Information ($I$), and Holevo quantity ($\chi$).
important_parameters: Cloning parameters ($	heta, \alpha, v$), and the local Bloch vectors characterizing the initial state $ho_{AB}$.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the specific adversarial model involving asymmetric, phase-variant cloning operations on the transmitted qubits.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate that the key rate remains positive ($r_D > 0$) for pure states and Werner states under single-qubit cloning attacks across defined parameter regimes.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing the necessary security metric ($r_D$), then analyzing the single-qubit cloning attack ($	ext{PC1QKD}$) for various state types, and finally contrasting these results with the more severe two-qubit cloning attack ($	ext{PC2QKD}$).
why_interesting: The rigorous application of key rate calculations to quantify security under specific, physically motivated attacks (cloning) provides a deeper understanding of the limitations of entanglement-based protocols beyond simple violation checks.
